newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea hiking reliance on W.African crude imports.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea hiking reliance on W.African crude imports.

text.p: South Korean oil refiners are becoming increasingly reliant on imports of West African crude oil following a flurry of refinery expansions in 1996, traders said on Wednesday.
"Imports of West African crude have risen following capacity expansions," said a crude trader at South Korea's largest oil refiner Yukong Ltd.
South Korea's total crude processing capability jumped to 2.44 million barrels per day (bpd) last year from 1.82 million bpd at the end of 1995.
Yukong and Hyundai Oil Refinery Co added 200,000-bpd capacity each and LG-Caltex Oil Corp 220,000 bpd.
But the expansion programme included little investment in units to reduce the sulphur content of oil products, forcing refineries to rely on crude that already has low sulphur.
And as Asia can no longer meet all of South Korea's needs for buying low sulphur crude, refineries are looking increasingly to West African producers, traders said.
"Tightening sulphur specification would keep local refiners looking to Africa for much needed low-sulphur crudes," said the Yukong trader.

"We have turned to West African crudes because we cannot get enough supplies from Southeast Asia," said a trader at Hanwha Energy Co, which purchased four million barrels of West African crude last year.
Governments throughout Asia are demanding oil products with lower and lower sulphur content to reduce environmental damage.

"Demand for low-sulphur crudes are likely to increase now that we are forced to reduce sulphur contents in our fuels," said a trader at Hyundai Oil, which bought three million barrels of West African crude last year.
The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said the sulphur content in fuel oil would be reduced to 0.5 percent from 1.0 percent starting in July 1997 in urban areas and 1999 in rural areas.
Last year, the ministry reduced the sulphur content in diesel, which is used as an industrial fuel as well as for home heating, to a maximum 0.1 percent from a previous 0.2 percent.
The sulphur content in diesel would be lowered again to a maximum of 0.05 percent in 1998 to meet levels in industrialised countries such as the United States or Japan.
Yukong purchased 18 million barrels of West African crude last year, more than half of the nation's total West African crude imports of 34.7 million barrels.
South Korea, which produces no crude oil, bought a total 721.9 million barrels of crude in 1996.
But with such a long-haul route between West Africa and South Korea, price will remain a major factor in determining the refiner's strategy.
"West African crude purchases would increase this year if the price spread between Dubai and Brent stays relatively narrow," the Yukong trader said.

The benchmark spread, used to determine the opportunity to import crude oil east of Suez, is currently falling and was assessed on Wednesday at $1.20/$1.30 -- a level currently considered economical for importing West African crudes into Asia.
However, when the price is closer to $2.00, West African crude is normally beyond the reach of buyers.
-- Seoul Newsroom (+822 727 5643)
